answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is a real passage from Marcus Aurelius’s ‘Meditations,’ Book IV, section 36 ↗. The thought is authentically his — but this exact English wording matches none of the standard published translations; it is a smoothed, modernized rendering closest to George Long’s classic 1862 line.

source.excerpt: Observe constantly that all things take place by change, and accustom thyself to consider that the nature of the Universe loves nothing so much as to change the things which are and to make new things like them. For everything that exists is in a manner the seed of that which will be.
trail: The passage is Marcus Aurelius, Meditations IV.36 ↗, here in George Long’s 1862 translation: “the nature of the Universe loves nothing so much as to change the things which are and to make new things like them.”

WIST’s side-by-side of 15 translations of 4.36 ↗ (Casaubon 1634 → Gill 2013) shows the same thought in every version — but none matches the popular “get used to thinking … existing forms” wording, including Staniforth (1964): “Observe how all things are continually being born of change.”
Wikiquote lists the line in its sourced Meditations, Book IV section ↗, confirming the attribution to Marcus Aurelius is genuine.
source.excerptNote: George Long’s public-domain 1862 translation of the full section IV.36. The viral wording (“Observe always that everything is the result of a change … get used to thinking … existing forms”) is a loosened modern paraphrase of this same passage.
source.rightsNote: The underlying passage is ancient (Greek, c. AD 170–180) and long in the public domain, and standard English translations such as George Long’s 1862 version are also public domain. But the exact wording quoted here matches no identifiable published translation — it is an anonymous modern web rendering — so no clear rights status can be assigned to this specific English text.

author.name: Marcus Aurelius
author.heading: About Marcus Aurelius
author.bio: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus was Roman emperor from AD 161 to 180 and the last of the so-called ‘Five Good Emperors.’ His Meditations — a private notebook written in Greek, never meant for publication — is one of the foundational texts of Stoic philosophy. Its recurring theme is the impermanence and constant transformation of all things, an idea he drew from Heraclitus and the Stoics; section IV.36 is one of its clearest statements.

misattribution.heading: Wording watch
misattribution.intro: The name is right — this really is Marcus Aurelius — but the wording is not any standard translation. Quote sites circulate a smoothed, editor-friendly version of Meditations IV.36 with no named translator.

items.why: The popular text — “Observe always that everything is the result of a change … get used to thinking that there is nothing Nature loves so well as to change existing forms” — matches none of the 15 catalogued translations ↗ of 4.36. It reads as a loosened web edit closest to George Long’s 1862 ending, “to make new things like them.”

Staniforth’s actual 4.36 reads “Observe how all things are continually being born of change,” not the viral phrasing, per the translation comparison ↗ — so crediting this exact wording to Staniforth is a mistake.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: the idea and the author are authentic Marcus Aurelius (Meditations IV.36 ↗); the exact English sentence is a modernized rendering of unknown editorial origin.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Section IV.36 sits at the heart of Stoic physics: the cosmos is a single, endlessly self-renewing process in which nothing is lost, only transformed. Marcus reminds himself that decay and death are not violations of nature but nature’s very method — “everything that exists is in a manner the seed of that which will be.”

The line travels well because it turns a hard fact into a consolation: change is not something Nature tolerates but something it ‘loves.’ That warmth is partly a gift of the loosened modern wording, which softens the sterner cadence of the older translations.
detailsBody: The Meditations were written in Koine Greek and circulated only after Marcus’s death. English versions run from Meric Casaubon (1634) through George Long (1862), the Loeb Haines (1916), Farquharson (1944), Staniforth (1964), Gregory Hays (2003) and beyond — each rendering 4.36 slightly differently. The wording most people quote today does not correspond to any one of these; it is a smoothed composite of uncertain origin.
context.pull: Nature loves nothing so much as to change existing forms and make new ones like them.
